extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning real analysis / rigorous calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and checking rigorous proofs of convergence/divergence for sequences and real-valued functions using quantified statements (ε–δ and N-based definitions), standard lemmas, and algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence as failure to converge to any L
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate divergence as the quantified statement: ∀L ∈ R, ∃ε > 0 s.t. ∀N ∈ N, ∃n ∈ N with (n > N) ∧ (|x_n − L| ≥ ε).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a sequence diverges you must handle an arbitrary L (not just show it fails to converge to one specific number). Typical strategy: pick a fixed ε (often ε = 1) and give an explicit construction of n > N (e.g. n = max{N, ⌈|L|⌉} + 1 or n = N+1) so that |x_n − L| ≥ ε. Consider cases for L (e.g. L ≤ 0 and L > 0) when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit constructive choices in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer giving an explicit choice (e.g. pick n = N+1 or n = max{N,⌈|L|⌉}+1) over vague existential phrasing (e.g. "some odd number larger than N").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statements like "let n be any odd number larger than N" are correct, supplying a simple explicit choice clarifies the proof and removes ambiguity in how n depends on N (good for readers and graders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: ε–δ limit of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of f as x approaches a is L iff ∀ε > 0, ∃δ > 0 s.t. (0 < |x − a| < δ) ⇒ (|f(x) − L| < ε).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always state and use the quantified ε–δ form when proving limits of functions. Explain the meaning in words (we can make f(x) arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to a, but not necessarily equal to a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the point x = a in the definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Require 0 < |x − a| < δ in the hypothesis so the definition concerns approaching a, not the value at a; f need not be defined at a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why x = a is excluded (limits describe approach, and derivatives or other constructions may require function undefined or different at the point). Don't mistakenly demand behavior at the point itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with scratchwork then write a concise proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do informal algebraic/scratch manipulations to discover a suitable choice of δ or n, then present a short formal proof that the chosen δ/n works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scratchwork may show various inequalities and motivate choices (e.g. δ = ε/3); the final written proof can omit the discovery steps but must verify the choice. It's usual for scratchwork to be longer than the polished proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose δ neatly for simple identities (f(x)=x)
rubrics_metrics.description: For proofs like lim_{x→a} x = a, a direct choice δ = ε suffices (many choices work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although infinitely many δ choices are valid (δ = ε/n etc.), pick a clean, simple δ for clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic simplification before δ selection (linear functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplify |f(x)−L| algebraically (e.g. |(3x+5)−(3a+5)| = 3|x−a|) to identify how ε controls |x−a| and choose δ accordingly (δ = ε/3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always simplify the target inequality to an expression involving |x−a|, then pick δ to make that expression < ε. This avoids overcomplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle reciprocals by bounding the independent variable near the point
rubrics_metrics.description: For expressions with denominators (e.g. 1/x), restrict x to a small neighborhood of the limit point (e.g. require |x−2|<1 so that 1<|x|<3) to bound |x| away from zero before manipulating inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot choose δ depending on x; instead impose an auxiliary constraint (e.g. δ ≤ 1) so that for all x in the δ-neighborhood a uniform bound on |x| holds. Then combine constraints via δ = min{..., ...}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use min to satisfy multiple δ (or N) constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When several conditions must hold simultaneously (e.g. |x−a|<1 and |x−a|<2ε), enforce both by picking δ = min{1, 2ε} (similarly N = max{...} for sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard way to make multiple uniform constraints true on the chosen neighborhood/threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove uniqueness of limits by triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a limit is unique, assume two limits K and L and use |K−L| = |(K−x_n) + (x_n−L)| ≤ |x_n−K| + |x_n−L| and let n be large to make the right-hand side arbitrarily small, concluding K = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the argument via arbitrary ε and invoke a lemma that if |K−L| < ε for every ε > 0 then K = L. This works both for sequences (N-based) and functions (δ-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: arbitrarily small distance implies equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If for every ε > 0 we have |K − L| < ε then K = L (proved by contrapositive: if K ≠ L take ε = |K−L|/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard lemma when deducing equality from an inequality that holds for all ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of limits: reduce to scalar and sum lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove c·lim and sum properties by first proving (i) c·x_n → c·a and (ii) x_n + y_n → a + b, then combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle the scalar multiple and sum as separate lemmas; be careful with the scalar case when c = 0 (either treat separately or avoid division by zero using |c|+1 tricks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalar multiple convergence (c·x_n → c·a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show |c x_n − c a| = |c|·|x_n − a| and choose ε_x = ε/|c| when c ≠ 0 (or handle c = 0 directly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid dividing by zero in a single-case proof, one can set ε_x = ε/(|c|+1) and proceed uniformly; explicitly treat c = 0 as trivial if preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum convergence via ε-splitting (ε/2 trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove x_n + y_n → a + b, pick ε_x = ε_y = ε/2 so that |(x_n+y_n) − (a+b)| ≤ |x_n−a| + |y_n−b| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ε/2 split is standard; more general splits (ε_x = αε, ε_y = βε with α+β ≤ 1) are also valid and sometimes useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of limits: algebraic decomposition and bounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite x_n y_n − a b = x_n(y_n − b) + b(x_n − a), apply the triangle inequality to get |x_n||y_n − b| + |b||x_n − a| and then bound |x_n| for large n via a preliminary lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because x_n is not constant, you must first show |x_n| is uniformly bounded near the limit (use a lemma choosing ε = |a|/2). Then pick ε-sizes carefully (denominators like 3|a|+1, 2|b|+1 are used in the book) to ensure each term < ε/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: bound sequence values near its limit
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n → a, then there exists N such that for n > N we have (|a|/2) ≤ |x_n| ≤ (3|a|/2) (proof uses reverse triangle inequality with ε = |a|/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is used to ensure denominators are nonzero and to produce uniform bounds on |x_n| or |f(x)| in neighborhoods where you need them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid division-by-zero with +1 denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing ε-based thresholds that involve dividing by |a| or |b|, use expressions like ε/(|c|+1) or ε/(2|b|+1) to avoid undefined operations if constants are zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pragmatic trick used throughout the proofs to produce uniform δ/N choices that work whether parameters are zero or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal limit proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 1/ y_n → 1/b (with b ≠ 0), rewrite |1/y_n − 1/b| = |y_n − b|/(|b||y_n|) and then ensure |y_n| is bounded away from zero (via lemma) and choose ε_y small enough to make the quotient < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the bound on |y_n| with a choice of ε_y = (|b|^2/2)·ε (book uses a particular form) and pick N large enough to enforce both |y_n − b| small and |y_n| away from zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio of limits by combining reciprocal and product results
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have 1/ y_n → 1/b, use product of limits to deduce x_n / y_n = x_n · (1/y_n) → a · (1/b) = a/b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure b ≠ 0 and that both component results (product and reciprocal) have been established under appropriate uniform bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous properties for function limits using δ instead of N
rubrics_metrics.description: All sequence-limit proofs and lemmas have direct analogues for limits of functions; replace thresholds N with neighborhoods δ and use the same decomposition and bounding techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting proofs, pick δ as the minimum of the required δ-constraints. Lemmas about bounding f(x) near K (analogous to Lemma 6.5.5) are used to avoid division-by-zero and obtain uniform bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on behavior near the limit; disregard distant points/small indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit proofs concentrate on what happens for sufficiently large n or for x sufficiently close to a; values at small n or far-away x are irrelevant to the limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state 'choose N (or δ) large (small) enough so that...' and note you need only ensure definitions hold beyond that threshold. This justifies ignoring finitely many initial terms or points outside the δ-neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: ε-splitting strategies and flexible allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple terms contribute to the error, split ε into parts (ε/2, ε/3, or general αε + βε with α+β ≤ 1) to control each part separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple equal splits (ε/2) when adequate; the text notes many choices are possible and sometimes picks denominators with +1 to avoid dividing by zero.
